content_metadata.description: This video explores the process of mRNA synthesis from double-stranded RNA genomes, with a focus on reoviruses as the primary example. It explains the mechanisms of viral replication, entry, and the unique strategies employed by these viruses.

qAndA.answer: Double-stranded RNA viruses must use their own enzyme because the plus strand is not accessible to ribosomes.
qAndA.question: Why do double-stranded RNA viruses need to bring in their own enzyme for mRNA synthesis?

qAndA.answer: Reoviruses possess two concentric icosahedral shells that facilitate mRNA synthesis within their core.
qAndA.question: What unique structural feature allows reoviruses to synthesize mRNA within their core?

qAndA.answer: mRNA is extruded from the viral core through fivefold symmetry axes.
qAndA.question: How do reoviruses release their mRNA into the cytoplasm?

qAndA.answer: Semi-conservative replication involves copying both strands of the template, while conservative replication uses only one strand.
qAndA.question: What is the difference between semi-conservative and conservative replication?

qAndA.answer: Reoviruses selectively use one strand of their RNA genome for mRNA synthesis, defining conservative replication.
qAndA.question: Why is the replication of reoviruses considered conservative?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Okay, one more class of viruses that have RNA genomes, the double stranded RNA viruses.
Remember these have to also bring in an enzyme because the plus part of the double stranded
RNA can't be accessed by ribosome. So what these guys do, they bring in a polymerase,
the polymerase makes mRNA from the double strands which can be translated and then eventually
it will take some of those mRNAs and make them double stranded to make new genome segments.
And these mRNAs are capped, they do not have poly, and not every Rio virus has a poly A
at the three prime end, some of them do. And these are very, this is a very simple copying.
The mRNAs are full length copies of the negative strand, so you have no issues with making up
the sequence. This is what these viruses look like, remember they're spherical and they
have two shells, they have two concentric icosahedral shells. And here's the intact
virion. And we talked last time about it as these viruses move through the endocytic pathway,
the outer shell gets digested away. So you're left with a core. And it's within this core
that the mRNA synthesis actually occurs. So here you can see the double stranded mRNAs,
the double stranded genome RNAs of these viruses, they're all packed into this core. And each
segment makes a single mRNA that makes a protein. You can see there are a lot of them here.
And again, all this happens in the particle. The RNAs never come out. So let's see how that
happens. Here is an infecting Rio virus. It gets taken into the cell by endocytosis, as
the endosome fuses with lysosomes. The outer shell is digested away. And eventually that
hydrophobic particle gets out of the endosome into the cytoplasm. And then it still has
its double stranded RNAs in it. You can see the green segments here. And the mRNA synthesis
begins. It's got the enzyme in the particle. And the RNAs come out of the fivefold axes
of symmetry. You can see them coming out here. They're capped in RNAs. So the enzyme stays
in the particle with the genome and the mRNAs extrude from the particle. And eventually
those mRNAs get translated. They form new particles with a single mRNA in each one. And then
those mRNAs get made double stranded inside the particle by the viral polymerase. And
then it leaves the cell. So the point here is that the virus particle not only brings the
enzyme in with each of these segments, but does all the synthesis within the particle.
So this is really a virus that never encodes. It never liberates its genome. This is just
a interesting cryoEM structure of rotavirus particles in the act of making mRNA. And you
can see here on the bottom. This is one fivefold axis of symmetry. And you can see an mRNA
coming out of the particle. Now the idea here is that below each fivefold axis of symmetry,
there's one segment and one enzyme. So each segment is located right below the fivefold
axis. And after it gets out of the endosome, that enzyme produces mRNA that's extruded
from the particles. It's really a neat method of doing this. Now because this is double
stranded, you may ask, is this conservative or semi-conservative? You know, when you replicate
DNA, when we replicate our DNA genomes, we do it in a semi-conservative fashion. That
is the two strands separate and then each one is duplicated. And so some of the double
stranded RNA viruses do this. But real viruses, the ones we've just been talking about, actually
do conservative replication. They take the genome, they make an mRNA from one strand and
then make that double stranded. So actually only one strand is being copied. So it's
called conservative replication.
